```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(occJSDM)
```

## What we want to know

Session 1 ended with a map of raw dhole detections and a doubt: a detection is not a presence. This session builds a model that answers the question properly. For each site, how likely is it that the dhole is really there, given everything we detected, and how sure are we?

## How the data are laid out

A two-stage eDNA model needs to know the survey's structure: PCR replicates sit inside field samples, and field samples sit inside sites. That structure is what lets it separate the presence of the animal from the detection of its DNA.

We read the same CSV files as in Session 1, keep all of `info` and only the dhole's column of `OTU`, and put the two in a list called `d`, the form `runOccJSDM()` expects.

```{r layout}
info <- read.csv("data-derived/info.csv")
OTU <- as.matrix(read.csv("data-derived/OTU.csv"))
dhole_col <- grep("Cuon_alpinus", colnames(OTU), value = TRUE)   # the dhole's column name in OTU
d <- list(info = info,
          OTU = OTU[, dhole_col, drop = FALSE])                   # drop = FALSE keeps OTU a matrix
str(d, max.level = 1)
dim(d$OTU)
```

Click on `d` in the Environment tab to open it.

- `d$info` is the table from Session 1, unchanged: one row per PCR replicate, with `Site`, `Sample`, the site covariates and the collection covariates.
- `d$OTU` is a matrix with the same 1,818 rows and a single column, the dhole. A 1 means the PCR was positive. It must stay a matrix with a column name, even with one species, which is why we write `drop = FALSE`.
- The rows of the two tables must be in the same order. Here they are, because both come from the same files.

Here is one site, laid out as the model sees it: three field samples, six PCRs each.

```{r one-site}
site_with_hits <- names(which.max(tapply(d$OTU[, 1], d$info$Site, sum)))
d$info |>
  mutate(positive = d$OTU[, 1]) |>
  filter(Site == site_with_hits) |>
  group_by(Sample) |>
  summarise(pcrs = n(), positive = sum(positive), .groups = "drop")
```

Two covariate sets matter. Occupancy covariates describe the site (climate, forest, human modification, region, and whether the stream rises inside the nature reserve). Collection covariates describe how a sample was taken (the volume of water filtered, rain the previous day), and can change whether DNA was caught at all.

## Fit the model

A fit for one species is fast, so we run it live. If the fit fails for any reason, the chunk says so and loads a saved copy of exactly the same fit, so you can carry on.

```{r fit, message = TRUE}
fit <- NULL
if (live_fit) {
  fit <- tryCatch({                              # try the live fit; on an error, run the second part
    set.seed(2026)
    runOccJSDM(
      data = d,
      listParams = list(n_factors = 0),          # one species, so no shared hidden factors
      threshold = 1,                             # a replicate is positive if its value is at least 1
      occCovariates = c("annual_precipitation", "mean_temperature", "Human_modification_1km",
                        "Percent_of_forest_cover_1km", "Patch_density_1km", "Edge_density_1km",
                        "streamOrigin", "Regional_Division"),
      collCovariates = c("Filter_vol", "PrevDayRain"),
      spatCovariates = character(),
      MCMCparams = list(nchain = 2, nburn = 5000, niter = 5000, nthin = 1),
      summarisedLatentPresences = TRUE
    )
  }, error = function(e) {
    message("The live fit failed: ", conditionMessage(e), "\nUsing the saved copy of the same fit instead.")
    NULL
  })
}
if (is.null(fit)) fit <- readRDS("data-derived/dhole_fit.rds")
```

## Can we trust the computation?

The model is fitted by MCMC, which explores possible parameter values. We must check that the two chains agree before reading anything.

```{r diagnostics}
diag <- returnConvergenceDiagnostics(fit)
head(diag)
c(parameters = nrow(diag),
  rhat_above_1.01 = sum(diag$rhat > 1.01, na.rm = TRUE),
  ess_below_400 = sum(diag$ess < 400, na.rm = TRUE))
diag |>
  filter(rhat > 1.01 | ess < 400) |>
  select(param, label1, mean, rhat, ess)
```

`diag` has one row per parameter. Open it in the Environment tab.

- `param` is the kind of parameter: `beta_psi` for the effect of an occupancy covariate, `p` and `q` for the true- and false-positive rates, and so on. `label1` (and `label2`, where needed) say which covariate or species it belongs to.
- `mean`, `sd`, `q2.5` and `q97.5` summarise the posterior: its mean, its spread, and the ends of its 95% interval.
- `rhat` compares the chains. Values near 1 mean they agree.
- `ess` counts how many independent draws the chains are worth. We want it large.

A flagged parameter is a reason to look closer, not to stop.

```{r traceplot}
draws <- fit$results_output$jsdm_output$B0_output   # species x iteration x chain
trace <- tibble(iteration = rep(seq_len(dim(draws)[2]), 2),
                chain = factor(rep(1:2, each = dim(draws)[2])),
                value = c(draws[1, , 1], draws[1, , 2]))
ggplot(trace, aes(iteration, value, colour = chain)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Trace of the baseline occupancy intercept",
       subtitle = "Two chains that overlap and wander around one level are a good sign",
       y = "Intercept") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Detection and false positives

The model estimates how often a PCR is positive when the dhole's DNA is in the sample (the true-positive rate), and how often it is positive when the dhole is not there (the false-positive rate).

```{r detection}
p_draws <- fit$results_output$p_output
q_draws <- fit$results_output$q_output
rates <- tibble(
  rate = c("True-positive rate", "False-positive rate (PCR)"),
  mean = c(mean(p_draws), mean(q_draws)),
  lower = c(quantile(p_draws, 0.025), quantile(q_draws, 0.025)),
  upper = c(quantile(p_draws, 0.975), quantile(q_draws, 0.975))
)
rates |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
p_in_ten <- round(10 * mean(p_draws))       # used in the text below
```

A PCR catches the dhole's DNA about `r p_in_ten` times in ten when it is there, and a stray positive is rare but not zero. That is why one positive PCR at a site is weak evidence on its own.

The convergence table above flagged the detection rates themselves: their R-hat is a little above 1.01 and their effective sample size is below 400. So the ends of these intervals rest on fewer effective draws than we would like. A longer run (raise `nburn` and `niter`) would pin them down more precisely. It would not make the intervals much narrower, because their width reflects how much the data say, not how long the chains ran. The conclusion that a single positive PCR is weak evidence does not depend on the exact numbers.

## Is the dhole at each site?

`computeConditionalOccupancyProbs()` returns a matrix with one row per site and one column per species (here only the dhole). Each value is the probability that the species is present at the site, given what was detected there. To map it, we need the site table from Session 1.

```{r probability}
cond <- computeConditionalOccupancyProbs(fit)
sites <- info |>
  distinct(Site, .keep_all = TRUE) |>                  # one row per site, as in Session 1
  select(-Sample, -Primer, -Filter_vol, -PrevDayRain) |>
  arrange(Site)
map_data <- sites |> mutate(probability = as.numeric(cond[Site, 1]))   # match by site name

ggplot(map_data, aes(Xs.1, Xs.2, colour = probability)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Probability the\ndhole is present", option = "C", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude",
       title = "The model's answer, site by site") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Each bar of the histogram below counts sites. Bars at the left are sites where the dhole is almost certainly absent, bars at the right where it is almost certainly present, and bars in the middle are sites the data cannot settle.

```{r certainty}
ggplot(map_data, aes(probability)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Probability the dhole is present at the site", y = "Number of sites",
       title = "Most sites are close to certain, one way or the other") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Compare this with Session 1's raw map. Many sites with a detection are now judged unlikely to hold a dhole, and a smaller set are close to certain. The model has not become vague. It has become sure about most sites, which is the kind of certainty the data support.

```{r certainty-count}
map_data |>
  mutate(verdict = cut(probability, c(-Inf, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, Inf),
                       labels = c("almost certainly absent", "probably absent",
                                  "probably present", "almost certainly present"))) |>
  count(verdict)
```

## What explains where the dhole is?

The harder question is why. We look at the effect of each site covariate on the chance the dhole is present.

```{r effects}
effects <- diag |>
  filter(param == "beta_psi") |>
  transmute(covariate = label1, mean, lower = q2.5, upper = q97.5)

ggplot(effects, aes(mean, covariate)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  labs(x = "Effect on the log-odds of presence", y = NULL,
       title = "Where the data are weak, intervals are wide") +
  theme_minimal()

detecting_sites <- sum(tapply(d$OTU[, 1], d$info$Site, sum) > 0)
crossing <- sum(effects$lower < 0 & effects$upper > 0)
c(detecting_sites = detecting_sites, effects = nrow(effects), intervals_crossing_zero = crossing)
```

How to read this figure:

- Each row is one covariate. The point is the best estimate of its effect, and the line is its 95% interval.
- For a number, such as `Human_modification_1km`, a positive effect means the dhole is more likely to be present where the covariate is higher.
- For a category, the effect compares one level with a reference level that does not get a row. `streamOriginoutsideGLGS` compares sites whose stream rises outside the Gaoligongshan reserve with those whose stream rises inside it. `Regional_DivisionNorthwest` and `Regional_DivisionSouthwest` compare those regions with the East.
- An interval that crosses the dashed line means we cannot tell whether the covariate matters.

With one species and `r detecting_sites` detecting sites, `r crossing` of the `r nrow(effects)` intervals cross the line.

Session 1 left a question open. In the ordination, sites inside the reserve and sites with little human modification lay at the same end of the plot, so the figure could not say which one species respond to. The model estimates the effect of each covariate with the others held fixed, so `streamOrigin` and `Human_modification_1km` are separated here. For the dhole alone, the data are too thin to say which matters. Session 3 asks the same question of all 108 mammals at once.

The mammal-wide fit of Session 3 does put one of the dhole's effects clearly away from zero.

```{r joint-effects}
joint_effects <- read_fit_summary()$effects |>
  filter(species == "Cuon alpinus") |>
  select(covariate, mean, lo, hi) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))
joint_effects
```

Its Southwest effect is clearly below zero. But do not set these numbers beside the one-species fit: they are measured after allowing for hidden site effects shared by all species, so they are on a different scale, and the intervals are mostly wider, not narrower. Being sure where the dhole is does not require being sure why.

Do the two fits at least agree about where the dhole is? Each point below is a site. Points on the grey line get the same probability from both fits.

```{r agreement}
joint <- read_fit_summary()$occ |>
  filter(species == "Cuon alpinus") |>
  select(Site, joint = cond_mean)
both <- map_data |>
  select(Site, single = probability) |>
  left_join(joint, by = "Site")
ggplot(both, aes(joint, single)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Mammal-wide fit", y = "One-species fit",
       title = "Both fits agree about where the dhole is") +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_equal()
round(cor(both$joint, both$single), 2)
```

```{r mcp, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !mcp_off}
1. Ask the assistant to check the data file `data-derived/dhole_input.rds` with `validate_data`, using the occupancy covariates `annual_precipitation`, `mean_temperature`, `Human_modification_1km`, `Percent_of_forest_cover_1km`, `Patch_density_1km`, `Edge_density_1km`, `streamOrigin` and `Regional_Division`, and the collection covariates `Filter_vol` and `PrevDayRain`. Ask it to explain any problem before fitting.
2. Ask it to fit the model with two chains of 5000 burn-in and 5000 kept iterations, no hidden factors, and a seed you choose.
3. Ask it for the convergence diagnostics, and compare its count of flagged parameters with yours.

If the assistant reports an error, tell your instructor and carry on with the code above. It does the same thing.
')
```

## What you take away

- A model that separates presence from detection can say where a species is and how sure it is.
- Check the chains before reading any number from the fit.
- The probability that the dhole is present at each site is firm for most sites. The reasons behind it are much less firm. Say both, honestly.
- Session 3 does this for all 108 mammals at once, and Session 4 turns the answers into a conservation plan.
